articles.title: AI leaders clash over safety fears after Anthropic whistleblower says AI could 'kill us all' by 2030
articles.text:
AI leaders clash over safety fears after Anthropic whistleblower says AI could 'kill us all' by 2030 — OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI figureheads call for external governance, while Jensen Huang says worries are 'made up'
Western Frontier model developers are all for it, but Open Weight proponents are far less keen.
This past week, employees and key figures at leading AI companies have called for a slowdown in the development of frontier AI models, citing warnings from their own teams and other AI researchers that the risk stemming from a super-intelligent AI could endanger the human race. However, while the top Western firms have shown solidarity on this issue, others have urged caution or downright denied their claims, but there's a deeper story within the calls for a slowdown, namely the tension between open-source and closed-source AI models.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the safety fears were "made up," and that there was no need for a slowdown. Chinese officials called the claims "fearmongering," and an effort to stymie international AI development efforts, while President Trump waded in with characteristic bombast and said that he was enough of an AI safeguard on his own, and that it was in the interests of China to enact a frontier AI slowdown
Meanwhile, other countries are reacting to the news and taking independent efforts to investigate AI safety, with the UK's King Charles setting a meeting with leading AI figureheads to discuss how to better develop AI for the benefit of humanity.
Why now?
If you ask most workers who've been scared into believing their livelihoods were in jeopardy, the time for AI slowdowns came and went years ago. Indeed, many are nostalgic for the time before AI. But why are so many tech leaders only now raising the alarm?
They claim it's entirely based around safety fears. Following months of AI seemingly surprising their own developers by breaching sandboxes to go on exploit-hunting sprees. The volume of concern rose considerably after former OpenAI researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned from Anthropic, claiming that none of the AI companies were taking AI safety and alignment seriously enough.
He didn't whistleblow on anything nefarious, dump documents or internal company data to prove his claims, or point to any specific attack vectors, or even actual harms. Instead, Coxon warned of a future potential of AI that he sees these companies racing towards without due concern.
What they're developing could, "kill us all by the end of the decade," he warned. It's not clear how, but it started a viral conversation all the same. Much like Matt Schumer's "Something big is happening" viral post from February this year.
Days later, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk showed surprising levels of solidarity for arch rivals in the space, putting out similar statements claiming that AI was becoming too powerful and that a general slowdown in the development of frontier AI models was the best solution.
Claiming that AI was playing an increasing role in improving itself — hinting at the recursive self-improvement (RSI) event that many AI researchers are concerned about — Amodei called for the creation of independent auditors for AI models. Altman agreed, even calling on governments to globalize the regulation to encourage unified compliance with any safety protocols enacted by the frontier developers.
Where we're going, we don't need roads
Not everyone feels these fears are warranted, however. China, which has recently made great strides in its development of highly intelligent open-weight models, called the concerns "fearmongering" and said it served no one's interest to be so confrontational. Although Chinese Premier Xi Jinping has said in the past that it was important for AI to "always remain under human control," the Chinese state-run Global Times paper called demands for a slowdown a method to "contain" Chinese developments.
Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has broken ranks with other Western AI leaders, claiming that there was no need for a slowdown and that any apocalyptic fears around AI were entirely fictional.
As one of the few companies making real — and enormous — profits from AI development, Nvidia has a vested interest in the expansion of the AI industry continuing on its current explosive trajectory. Indeed, it has heavily invested in it. Nvidia has stakes in hardware and software companies, along with providing backstops for neo-cloud firms. It also recently bought Hugging Face for $13 billion.
We've been here before
While the AI CEOs might have suddenly decided it's time to slow down, there have been many, many others who have made that call before now. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders has been at the forefront of claims that the AI industry was moving too fast and breaking too many things, and recently called for heavy prison sentences for those developing superintelligent AI.
Over 1,000 AI workers signed an open letter in July this year calling on the U.S. government to control AI research and ensure safety and security. Others did that in 2023, too. This isn't even the first time that AI CEOs have called for slowdowns on AI development. Dario Amodei called for global coordination to police AI after the release of OpenAI's GPT2 model in 2019. Elon Musk did the same in 2023.
None of this takes away from the real dangers of AI, or the suggestion that now may really be the time to do something about them. But it does raise questions about the reasons behind their coordinated fear-raising. Even if it isn't fear-mongering.
Safety, or a trojan horse?
The collation of leading Western frontier AI companies clamoring for tighter controls over powerful AI models has another theoretical benefit too: containing the number of AI models that are permitted for use in the Western Hemisphere. A cursory look at OpenRouter's AI model rankings, which base themselves on the total number of tokens generated, places just three Western-made models on the top ten list — the heavily discounted GPT 5.6 Luna at number one, Nvidia's Nemotron Ultra 3 (Free) at number eight, and Google's recently-launched Gemini 3.8 Flash at number ten.
The rest of the models in the rankings are all open-weight Chinese models, which, more often than not, are cheaper than leading Western frontier models, according to the Artificial Analysis' Cost per Intelligence index. The Chinese models in OpenRouter's current top ten include Z.AI's GLM 5.3, Deepseek V4 Flash, and Tencent's Hy4 and Hy3. So, if the development of a Western frontier AI alliance emerges under the guise of calls for safety, it's possible that said companies are aiming to be the chosen few, creating a closed-loop monopoly for "preferred" AI providers. However, this remains speculation as the situation develops.
Will anything actually change?
Although the major AI companies may voluntarily, or even jointly, throttle their development efforts to improve safety, enacting anything globally significant will need the cooperation of international governments. There are certainly calls from politicians the world over to rein in the trillion-dollar companies and their cutting-edge autonomous systems.
But with the U.S. government firmly on the side of limited regulation, and no clear indication of what a slowdown would even look like. Would that entail limited compute? No new models? A halt to superintelligence research? It's hard to imagine a global consensus taking shape as things stand.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: Govt sets 0.4% fee on UPI merchant payments above Rs 2,000; caps charge at Rs 300
articles.text:
Govt sets 0.4% fee on UPI merchant payments above Rs 2,000; caps charge at Rs 300
The move ends the zero-MDR regime that has been in place since January 2020, introduced to drive digital payments adoption but long criticised by banks and fintechs as unsustainable.
The government has set a 0.4% charge on UPI payments above Rs 2,000 to merchants and capped the fee at Rs 300 for payments of Rs 75,000 and above as it rolled out a framework for large digital merchant payments.
The move ends the zero-MDR (merchant discount rate) regime that has been in place since January 2020, introduced to drive digital payments adoption but long criticised by banks and fintechs as unsustainable.
Essential sectors like railways, telecom and fuel get a flat Rs 5 fee per transaction, while capital markets get a lighter 0.02% rate.
Small merchants earning up to Rs 1 lakh a month via UPI QR codes stay fully exempt - a carve-out the government says shields 96% of merchant transactions from any new charge, an official statement said.
MDR on person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, have been capped at Rs 300 for payments of Rs 75,000 and above.
Person-to-merchant transactions up to Rs 2,000 remain outside the scope of MDR.
Person-to-person transfers—37% of UPI's volume and 70% of its value—remain untouched. Consumers can continue to transact free of cost using UPI.
App providers are barred from adding platform fees, and banks have been told not to let merchants pass MDR costs to customers. A fifth of the new fee pool will fund small-merchant UPI expansion.

articles.title: Los estudiantes usan IA para hacer trampas. Ahora pierden horas intentando que no se note
articles.text:
Antes de la IA, los estudiantes ya copiaban en exámenes, se descargaban trabajos de 'El Rincón del Vago' o incluso pagaban para que alguien se los hiciera. Con la IA, hacer trampas se ha convertido en algo tan sencillo y cotidiano que la comunidad educativa está tomando cartas en el asunto. Pero los profesores no son tontos, cuando un alumno usa IA lo notan, y por eso cada vez más alumnos se esfuerzan en hacer que no cante tanto. Bienvenidos a la guerra entre quienes hacen trampas con IA y quienes las detectan.
Detectar la IA. A estas alturas de la película, si ChatGPT hace un trabajo de clase y el alumno lo entrega tal cual, es muy probable que el profesor le acabe pillando. Ya somos capaces de detectar las típicas frases y palabras que suele usar la IA, se pueden colar alucinaciones y datos sin verificar. Además, hay muchas universidades que recurren a softwares antiplagio como Turnitin que también cuentan con detectores de IA.
Estos detectores no son muy fiables y hasta la propia Turnitin reconoce que existen los falsos positivos, planteando sus resultados como una señal para que el profesor investigue el caso, no como un veredicto automático. Las sospechas suelen venir de detalles más sutiles, como un cambio brusco de estilo, referencias que el alumno no sabe defender o una entrega demasiado impecable.
Solución: disimularla. Está la opción de usar herramientas "humanizadoras" de textos, cuyo objetivo es eliminar las típicas frases y palabras que suele usar la IA para que no sea tan evidente, pero hay alumnos que prefieren dedicar tiempo a revisar y reescribir los textos de la IA para que parezcan suyos.
En el New York Magazine han entrevistado a varios alumnos que cuentan sus trucos, como Will, que reescribe todo el texto línea por línea para que no se note que ha usado Claude para redactarlo. O Theo, que encargó una presentación de astronomía a Codex y quedó tan perfecta que tuvo que pasar cuatro horas "estropeándola" para que pareciera hecha por un alumno de su nivel. "Requirió mucho trabajo", dijo el alumno. Quizás habría terminado antes haciendo el trabajo él mismo.
Sofisticando las trampas. A medida que las universidades implementan obstáculos para hacer trampas, los estudiantes también descubren trucos para sortearlas. En la Universidad de Nueva York utilizan una plataforma llamada WebAssign cuyo objetivo es dificultar mucho las trampas a la hora de completar tareas, pero ya lo dice el refrán: hecha la ley, hecha la trampa. Un alumno creó un bot para ir rellenando las respuestas de forma lenta y errática, imitando el ritmo de un estudiante para que así no resultara sospechoso. Después lo compartió con otros compañeros.
La paradoja es que hacer trampas ya no consiste simplemente en pedirle algo a ChatGPT y pegar la respuesta: puede requerir revisar, reescribir o incluso programar lo suficiente para que el resultado parezca humano.
Desconfianza. Es lo que la IA ha provocado en el sector educativo y hay un ejemplo que lo ilustra muy bien. La Universidad de Princeton presumía de confiar tanto en el honor de sus estudiantes que no ponían vigilancia en los exámenes. Eso se ha acabado y en mayo de este año anunciaron que empezarían a supervisar los exámenes presenciales, poniendo fin a una política que databa de 1893, más de un siglo.
¿Y si la solución no es perseguir? Hay quien cree que la solución al problema sea crear detectores más potentes o poner más vigilancia. En declaraciones a New York Magazine, Danielle Carr, profesora de UCLA, sostiene que la IA no es "un problema técnico con una solución técnica" y si los estudiantes quieren hacer trampas, van a encontrar la manera. Su apuesta pasa por diseñar clases y evaluaciones en las que aprender compense más que delegar el trabajo.
Algunas universidades españolas ya ensayan modelos con distintos niveles de uso: prohibida en asignaturas básicas, permitida con transparencia en otras y obligatoria en proyectos avanzados, donde el alumno debe demostrar que entiende y sabe evaluar lo que produce la herramienta. Alberto Sols, director de la Escuela de Arquitectura, Ingeniería, Ciencia y Computación dice que la IA puede ser un “exoesqueleto intelectual”, pero primero hay que saber caminar sin él.

articles.title: Un canular ! Trump balaie le risque d’extinction par l’IA comme le réchauffement climatique
articles.text:
Donald Trump rejette les scénarios d’une intelligence artificielle capable de menacer l’humanité et les rapproche de ce qu’il appelle « l’arnaque du réchauffement climatique ». Au moment où plusieurs figures de l’IA réclament davantage de prudence, le président américain estime surtout qu’un dirigeant comme lui constitue le meilleur garde-fou.
Pour protéger l’humanité d’une intelligence artificielle devenue incontrôlable, Donald Trump a une solution toute trouvée : lui-même. Rien que ça. Dans une série de messages publiés le 14 septembre sur son réseau Truth Social, le président américain a qualifié de « canular » les scénarios dans lesquels l’IA finirait par détruire l’humanité, avant de les rapprocher de ce qu’il appelle l’« arnaque du réchauffement climatique ».
Une réponse pour le moins expéditive aux inquiétudes exprimées depuis plusieurs années par ceux-là mêmes qui développent les modèles les plus puissants du marché.
Trump s’érige en garde-fou de l'IA
Le raisonnement présidentiel accorde surtout une place centrale à son auteur. Selon Donald Trump, la meilleure protection serait « un président FORT ET INTELLIGENT (QI élevé !) » (sic). Un profil dont les États-Unis disposeraient évidemment déjà, à l’en croire.
Il dénonce dans le même temps une offensive contre l’intelligence artificielle et les centres de données américains, qui profiterait avant tout à la Chine. Le débat sur la sûreté et l’encadrement des modèles se retrouve donc ramené à une affaire de leadership politique…
La comparaison avec le climat brouille encore davantage le message. Le réchauffement provoqué par les activités humaines repose sur un consensus scientifique solidement établi. Une extinction de l’humanité provoquée par une IA reste, elle, un scénario hypothétique dont la probabilité et les mécanismes font débat. Mettre les deux dans le même sac sous l’étiquette de « canular » ne répond donc pas aux faits établis sur le climat ni aux interrogations bien réelles sur la sûreté des IA.
Des appels à ralentir qui ne datent pas d’hier
Ces inquiétudes ne sont pas nouvelles. En mars 2023, une lettre ouverte du Future of Life Institute, signée notamment par Elon Musk, demandait une pause d’au moins six mois dans l’entraînement des systèmes plus puissants que GPT-4.
Deux mois plus tard, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei et Demis Hassabis figuraient parmi les signataires d’un texte appelant à traiter le risque d’extinction lié à l’IA comme une priorité mondiale, au même titre que les pandémies ou la guerre nucléaire. Sans réclamer, cette fois, l’arrêt des entraînements.
Le débat a ressurgi le 12 septembre 2026, lorsque Dario Amodei a proposé de ralentir de manière coordonnée le développement des modèles de pointe afin de laisser aux dispositifs de sécurité le temps de suivre. Sam Altman et Elon Musk ont soutenu cette démarche, qui prévoit notamment davantage d’évaluations indépendantes, sans réclamer l’arrêt des entraînements.
Donald Trump, lui, ne veut manifestement pas entendre parler de freinage. Là où une partie de l’industrie demande davantage de ceintures de sécurité, le président américain préfère surtout rappeler qui, selon lui, doit tenir le volant.

articles.title: Pour dépister la cataracte, un simple smartphone pourrait suffire
articles.text:
Pour dépister la cataracte, un simple smartphone pourrait suffire
Le dépistage de la cataracte et d'autres maladies oculaires pourrait faire un bond de géant grâce à un nouveau système basé sur un simple smartphone Android. Une bonne nouvelle, notamment pour les personnes vivant dans des zones reculées.
En 2026, la cataracte demeure la principale cause de cécité dans le monde, touchant près de 100 millions de personnes. Le Dr Prabhu Krishna Ravilla, médecin à l’Aravind Eye Hospital de Madurai (Inde), a pris la parole lors du 44e Congrès de la Société européenne des chirurgiens de la cataracte et de la chirurgie réfractive (ESCRS), ce dimanche 13 septembre. Il y a présenté les résultats d'une étude très prometteuse pour endiguer ce fléau, notamment dans les zones du globe où les ophtalmologues manquent cruellement.
Un système simple et fiable pour détecter la cataracte
Le médecin et ses collègues ont mis au point un système accessible afin de faire mieux que les “camps de la vue”, des cliniques temporaires de dépistage coûteuses et complexes à mettre en place, qui ne touchent généralement qu'une part réduite de la population.
Le docteur précise d’ailleurs qu’“une étude antérieure menée par l’hôpital ophtalmologique Aravind a révélé que les campagnes de dépistage ne permettaient d’examiner que 7 % des habitants des zones rurales ciblées. La fréquentation chute de 80 % chez les personnes résidant à plus de 3 km. Et parmi celles qui ne s’y sont pas rendues, un tiers avait besoin d’une opération de la cataracte. Les femmes, les personnes âgées et les communautés les plus pauvres sont les plus défavorisées. La pandémie de Covid-19 a aggravé la situation en entraînant l’arrêt des activités de proximité.”
Une formation de 3 h et un équipement à moins de 175 €
Le système pour pallier ces difficultés est on ne peut plus simple. Basé sur un smartphone Android, il s'agit d'une pince à clipser sur le capteur photo dorsal. Une lentille grossissante, deux leds alimentées par le téléphone et un embout en silicone permettent d'obtenir une image claire et isolée de la lumière extérieure de l'œil sur lequel l'ensemble est posé. Le coût de la solution serait de moins de 175 €, smartphone compris.
Une app mobile, conçue notamment pour la télémédecine, accompagne le tout, tandis qu'une formation de 3 h suffit pour maîtriser l'appareil. Dans le cadre de l'étude, 1093 patients ont été dépistés et un protocole a été mis en place pour vérifier l'efficacité du dispositif. Les diagnostics des ophtalmologues présents sur place ont ainsi été comparés à ceux de confrères à distance, disposant des données récoltées par les smartphones.
L’IA pour accélérer les futurs diagnostics ophtalmologiques
Dans 96 % des cas, les médecins sont tombés d'accord sur la nécessité — ou non — d'envoyer un patient à l'hôpital pour des examens supplémentaires. Pour un diagnostic de cataracte pur, le taux de concordance s'est élevé à 89 %.
Cette solution ne remplace donc pas un examen clinique complet, mais prouve qu'il n'est pas forcément nécessaire qu'un spécialiste soit physiquement présent pour établir un premier diagnostic. Portable et peu coûteuse, cette technologie peut aider les professionnels de santé à dépister beaucoup plus de personnes en se déplaçant directement dans les zones isolées.
Pour le Dr. Ravilla, qui évoque également un futur système basé sur l'IA pour classifier les données collectées et réduire ainsi la dépendance aux examens à distance : “Pour les décideurs politiques et les responsables de la planification en matière de santé publique, cette plateforme offre une piste pour étendre le dépistage de la cataracte sans augmentation proportionnelle des effectifs de spécialistes. La plateforme s’intègre à l’infrastructure existante des agents de santé communautaires, fonctionne dans des environnements à faible bande passante et a démontré son acceptabilité auprès des patients.”

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: cuáles son las diferencias entre los dos teléfonos de Apple
articles.text:
Ya tenemos todos los detalles de la nueva generación de teléfonos de Apple: iPhone 18 Pro y el iPhone 18 Pro Max, dos equipos que mantienen la línea estética de sus antecesores pero incorporan cambios de fondo en procesador, cámaras y autonomía.
La marca permitirá reservar ambos modelos a partir del 12 de septiembre, mientras que la llegada a tiendas está prevista para el 18 de septiembre. Frente a los iPhone 17 Pro y 17 Pro Max, las diferencias no son solo cosméticas.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuáles son las diferencias de diseño y pantalla
El chasis en aluminio se mantiene como base en ambas generaciones, así como el módulo de triple cámara trasera. Sin embargo, el grosor en la zona de los sensores aumenta levemente para alojar las nuevas ópticas.
El peso también sube unos gramos, resultado de una batería de mayor capacidad y de un sistema de cámara de vapor mejorado para su refrigeración. Pese a estos ajustes, las fundas del iPhone 17 Pro siguen siendo compatibles con el nuevo modelo.
PUBLICIDAD
En el iPhone 18 Pro, la trasera de cristal se unifica en tono con el marco de aluminio, lo que elimina el contraste bicolor del año pasado. La paleta de colores suma el tono Cereza oscuro junto al Azul Cielo y el Plata clásico.
La pantalla pasa a tecnología LTPO+, pensada para reducir el consumo energético sin afectar brillo ni fluidez. El iPhone 18 Pro además reduce el tamaño de la Dynamic Island, algo que no ocurre en el iPhone 18 Pro Max, cuyo panel conserva las mismas dimensiones que el modelo anterior.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuáles son las mejoras de rendimiento del iPhone 18 Pro y Pro Max
El cambio más relevante es el nuevo procesador A20 Pro, fabricado con arquitectura de dos nanómetros. Se trata del primer chip de este tipo en un teléfono inteligente, algo similar al M6 que ya utiliza el Mac Mini.
La diferencia entre versiones aparece en la GPU: el iPhone 18 Pro Max incorpora ocho núcleos gráficos, mientras que el iPhone 18 Pro se queda en siete, enfocados al procesamiento de inteligencia artificial y a juegos exigentes. Apple promete un 18% más de rendimiento y hasta un 30% más de eficiencia energética frente al A19 Pro de la generación anterior de teléfonos.
PUBLICIDAD
Estas son las mejoras en la cámara del iPhone 18 Pro
El salto fotográfico es compartido por ambas versiones Pro. La cámara principal de 48 megapíxeles estrena apertura variable, un mecanismo físico que regula la entrada de luz al sensor y mejora el control de la profundidad de campo en disparos nocturnos.
Apple también rediseñó la aplicación de Cámara para permitir el ajuste manual de esa apertura. El teleobjetivo gana luminosidad en ambos casos, con capturas de larga distancia de mayor definición y menor ruido.
PUBLICIDAD
La cámara frontal del iPhone 18 Pro Max sube a 25 megapíxeles, frente a los 18 megapíxeles que conserva el iPhone 18 Pro, que es igual a la del modelo de 2025.
Cómo mejora la batería y la autonomía
La combinación del chip A20 Pro con la pantalla LTPO+ eleva la duración de batería en toda la gama. El iPhone 18 Pro Max promete hasta 45 horas de reproducción de video, frente a las horas de autonomía del modelo del año pasado.
PUBLICIDAD
El iPhone 18 Pro, por su parte, alcanza hasta 36 horas de reproducción de video, por encima de las 31 horas del iPhone 17 Pro. La carga rápida permite llegar al 50% de batería en 15 minutos en el modelo Pro Max.
iPhone 18 Pro aumenta los precios frente al iPhone 17 Pro
El aumento de precio afecta a toda la línea Pro. Según Apple para los modelos base de 256 GB, el iPhone Pro pasó de USD 1.099 a USD 1.199, un incremento de 100 dólares.
PUBLICIDAD
El iPhone Pro Max siguió el mismo patrón: de USD 1.199 a USD 1.299. En el mercado europeo, el modelo más básico del iPhone 18 Pro Max parte de 1.619 euros, 150 euros por encima del iPhone 17 Pro Max.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: GM gives its most important trucks a new UI—and includes CarPlay
articles.text:
General Motors is about to launch new versions of its bestselling Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra pickup trucks for model year 2027, and among the changes are new user interfaces for the trucks’ digital displays. The automaker has gone for a more minimalist approach than we’ve seen from it in the past, and after a demo yesterday, it seems like it has been listening to constructive feedback to improve the products. And yes, unlike GM’s electric vehicles, these trucks still let you cast your Apple or Android phone to the infotainment system.
Although GM showed us video of the main instrument cluster—the gauges and info that’s presented to the driver—we don’t have any screenshots we can show you. But I was impressed with the restraint and lack of visual noise; instead, the background is always black, which should be dark even at night thanks to local dimming technology.
There are a number of different views. One with simple half-moon dials for speed and engine rpm; on the right side of the display is a user-configurable zone, where you can browse your music or audio feeds, display trip info, or turn-by-turn directions. Another is a driver assist display, with green as the highlight color to show when Super Cruise is active; this shows you a representation of what the car’s fused sensors are seeing around it. A third is for off-road driving, with your various angles and diff settings, and a fourth is for towing.
Note the real controls for the HVAC.
Credit:
GM
Note the real controls for the HVAC.
Credit:
GM
But there’s also an even more minimalist version that simply shows the speed as big white digits and nothing else. This is similar to the night mode you’d find in Saabs, and it’s very useful for night driving.
At the base of the main instrument display is a strip of information that’s permanently displayed regardless of the view mode you choose—this includes things like your fuel level, the drive mode, and any warning lights that may appear.
Yes, it has CarPlay
The central infotainment screen still runs on Android Automotive OS, but now the home screen is a more useful split view showing the music and navigation apps, with a full map view rather than the limited map that GM previously showed in its split-screen view. “If you wanted to search something or provide feedback on road conditions or something like that, when you tapped on the screen, it took you out of the home screen and took you to the full-screen maps. Here, you can do everything that full-screen maps can do right inside this window,” said Colin McCormick, group product manager at GM.
A dedicated row at the bottom of the screen is for the climate controls, although, as you’ll note from the photos, there are physical dials to change the temperature, as well as physical buttons for fan speed and demisting.
GM has also integrated more Android-like notifications into the infotainment system and included the ability to create quick actions. It has also changed the behavior of some of its apps—now, if you accept a phone call, it won’t switch you out of whatever app was active to dump you into the dialer app anymore.
Here’s what Apple CarPlay looks like. The card on the left shows towing information.
GM
Here’s what Apple CarPlay looks like. The card on the left shows towing information.
GM
Here’s what Android Auto looks like. Here, the card shows trip info.
GM
Here’s what Android Auto looks like. Here, the card shows trip info.
GM
Here’s what Apple CarPlay looks like. The card on the left shows towing information.
GM
Here’s what Android Auto looks like. Here, the card shows trip info.
GM
GM made the decision to drop Apple CarPlay and Android Auto phone casting from its newer EVs, and it’s one we’ve been pretty critical of. Although the automaker told us it made that decision in order to offer a better, more unified experience to its customers, that may well have changed: here, customers still have the choice to just cast their phone to the center screen.
And it has done a better job of integrating CarPlay and Android Auto into the experience, putting the casting apps in a large window or tile that takes up most but not all of the infotainment screen. To the left is another card that allows you to access other native apps, like towing or music (although you can still have CarPlay as the source for that native music app, should you start feeling a little Inceptionish). Porsche took a similar approach to working with, rather than against, users who enjoy CarPlay, and this looks like a welcome step from GM.
GM’s spokesperson wouldn’t be drawn on whether this means we’re going to see a corporate retreat from the previous stance on EVs, but I will note that the press release it sent Ars does say that the system was built “as a single scalable foundation across electric, gas and diesel-powered vehicles, it transforms time spent behind the wheel into an effortless, personalized journey,”—emphasis mine.
Passenger screens are here to stay
Complaining about the trend of OEMs putting an extra infotainment screen in the dash for the front passenger is evidently a losing battle now, because such a feature will be available on the Sierra and Silverado. The screen is coated in a polarized filter, so the driver can’t see what they’re doing or watch what they’re watching.
There are lots of native streaming apps now. The lower trim piece folds down to show more of the screen.
Credit:
GM
There are lots of native streaming apps now. The lower trim piece folds down to show more of the screen.
Credit:
GM
This can be streaming content or video piped in via HDMI from a port down by the passenger’s knee. And the passenger infotainment screen will pair with Bluetooth headphones so the driver doesn’t necessarily have to listen to whatever it is, either. (Some information will show up on the main infotainment screen, so the driver will have an idea of what content is playing on the screen and decide whether to pass through audio to the truck’s speakers, GM told us.) It’s not just for watching video, though—there’s even a full web browser, and you can use your smartphone as a keyboard or input device.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

articles.title: Steam Deck 2 Plans Haven't Changed Despite RAM Crisis, Claims Valve
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 15th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Steam Deck 2 Plans Haven't Changed Despite RAM Crisis, Claims Valve
Valve has confirmed that the ongoing DRAM shortage hasn't changed anything about its plans for a Steam Deck 2, even though the crisis has driven up prices on the company's other hardware. Speaking with IGN's Jacqueline Thomas, Valve developer Pierre-Loup Griffais was asked directly whether the memory shortage had affected the next handheld's development. Here's what he told IGN:
"We've talked before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, and I think we're still looking at it in the same way. It's just a matter of looking at the current conditions and seeing how and when we can deliver something like that. But from what we're working on, as far as the user experience goes and what the product that we're trying to build goes, it's very similar goals."
It is important to remember the context behind Valve's recent hardware launches. The Steam Machine ended up at $1,049 for its base model, and the Steam Frame launched at $1,059, both well above what Valve had reportedly hoped to charge before memory prices spiked. Griffais admitted pricing has likely dented demand for those two products, though he said it's hard to quantify how much. For the Steam Deck 2, Valve says the crisis hasn't had a significant impact on development plans, at least for now. That pressure might eventually reach the Steam Deck 2, since its release is still some ways away and Valve still hasn't given any indication of a launch window yet.
		
		Source:
				Valve via IGN			
	
	
	
		
	
		
"We've talked before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, and I think we're still looking at it in the same way. It's just a matter of looking at the current conditions and seeing how and when we can deliver something like that. But from what we're working on, as far as the user experience goes and what the product that we're trying to build goes, it's very similar goals."

articles.title: The Poco F9 Ultra is so powerful and long-lasting that I can forgive the price hike over its predecessor
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Poco F9 Ultra builds on its predecessor's excellent blueprint by ditching the denim look and upgrading some internals. This is a phone that competes with Samsung and Google flagships on price but more than delivers with top performance, a great screen and speakers, and stellar gaming ability to boot.
Pros
- +Exemplary performance and gaming chops
- +Enormous battery with fast charging
- +Well priced for the specs despite price rise
Cons
- -Despite still being great value, it costs more than the F8 Ultra
- -Cameras are capable but not top-tier
Why you can trust TechRadar
Poco F9 Ultra: Two-minute review
Poco’s latest high-end phone, the Poco F9 Ultra, continues to show you don’t have to spend absolute top dollar to get the best performance — but a price increase over the previous-generation model is hard to ignore.
The F9 Ultra replaces the Poco F8 Ultra after less than a year, and with the same chipset and design, it doesn’t change too much at first glance. But look deeper, and this is a refined upgrade that boasts an enormous battery bringing multi-day power, a new 200MP main camera sensor, and some of the best speakers on any phone.
The whole package proves you don’t have to spend four figures to land a phone with top-of-the-line specs and performance. The base model with 12GB RAM and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset costs $799 / £899 — yes, that's a $70 / £150 increase over the starting price of the F8 Ultra, but Poco did explain to TechRadar that it believes this new price remains "competitive" for the level of specs on offer. And it has a point — there are only a handful of phones offering 12GB RAM and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset for less money (one of which is Poco's own F8 Ultra).
The F9 Ultra's massive 6.9-inch AMOLED display looks great and is capable of 185Hz refresh rates during compatible games. Gameplay is also boosted with the unusual addition of a Bose-tuned subwoofer on the back, plus you're getting dual speakers, which makes the F9 Ultra a top choice for hands-free calls and listening to podcasts without headphones (though I still can’t condone blasting music from it here are on principle).
As mentioned, for those after the latest Snapdragon silicon for as little money as possible, the F9 Ultra is only undercut by Poco's own F8 Ultra, or indeed the Xiaomi 17, which launched for £899 but is currently on sale for £699. But the F9 Ultra still costs a whopping $500 / £380 less than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, and it wipes the floor with the pricier Google Pixel 11 Pro XL when it comes to gaming.
The cherry on top is a mammoth 8,050mAh battery, one of the biggest on a flagship device available in the UK at the time of writing (September 2026). It means the F9 Ultra can last for three days with moderate use, and I found it impossible to kill in a waking day.
And lastly, aside from a slightly stingy four years of Android updates, six years of security patches to see you through to 2032 is good to see on a phone as well-rounded as this.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Poco F9 Ultra review: Price and availability
- Starts at £899 / $799 / €1,099.99
- A $70 / £150 price increase on the F8 Ultra
- Not officially available in Australia
- Still competitive considering the specs
The Poco F9 Ultra starts at $799 / £749, though the US price varies depending on the seller (the phone is not officially available through US carriers, but $799 is Poco's official US price). Official UK availability is good to see, though £749 represents a £150 increase on the F8 Ultra’s £749 starting price, and at the time of writing, the older model is on sale for £649, which is an absolute steal.
But in being equipped with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, the F9 Ultra undercuts the Galaxy S26 Ultra — the only S26 series phone in the UK to run a Qualcomm chipset — by an almighty £380, and it's much less than the £1,279 Pixel 11 Pro XL, too, whose Tensor G6 chipset can’t hold a candle to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in terms of performance.
In fact, at £899, the F9 Ultra is the same price as the Google Pixel 11, but it offers superior gaming chops, a more expansive display, and much better battery life. That's why, despite increasing the price, Poco believes the F9 Ultra remains "competitive" in today's market — and we're inclined to agree.
- Value Score 4 / 5
Poco F9 Ultra review: Specs
Here’s a look at the Poco F9 Ultra’s key specs:
| Row 0 - Cell 0 | Poco F9 Ultra | 
| Dimensions: | 163.5 x 77.9 x 8.7mm | 
| Weight: | 235g | 
| Display: | 6.9-inch AMOLED | 
| Resolution: | 1200 x 2608 | 
| Refresh rate: | 185Hz | 
| Peak brightness: | 10,000 nits | 
| CPU: | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | 
| RAM: | 12GB/16GB | 
| Storage: | 256GB/512GB/1TB | 
| OS: | HyperOS 3, based on Android 16 | 
| Main cameras: | 200MP main (f/1.7), 50MP ultra-wide (f/2.4), 50MP 5x telephoto (f/3.0) | 
| Selfie camera: | 32MP (f/2.2) | 
| Battery: | 8,050mAh | 
| Charging: | 100W wired, 50W wireless | 
| Colors: | Dark Cherry, Black | 
Poco F9 Ultra review: Design
- Similar look to the iPhone 17 Pro
- Large but manageable device
- Sleek dark cherry colour replaces gaudy denim
The Poco F9 Ultra I reviewed is the lovely Dark Cherry option, which I prefer over the F8 Ultra’s bold but gaudy Denim Blue. Despite being a very large phone, the F9 Ultra is very comfortable to hold thanks to subtly curved aluminum side rails and a ‘Glass Fibre’ composite rear, which should be more resilient than the glass found on most rival flagship devices.
There’s also a black model if you'd prefer a safer option, with a red power button for a pop of color. The Dark Cherry variant hardly shows any fingerprints on its matte surface, and the overall look of the F9 Ultra grew on me in the weeks I was testing it, despite its obvious similarities with the iPhone 17 Pro and indeed the F8 Ultra.
The phone's four-circle camera design alongside the Bose-branded subwoofer is different enough to me, and manages to look as simplistic as possible. The F9 Ultra also doesn’t rock and wobble when used face up on a table, which is a nice touch.
Save for the one-piece volume rocker above the power button on the right edge, there isn't much else to report besides a USB-C port and speaker grilles on the top and bottom. When all is said and done, this is quite a conservative design when it’s not clad in faux denim!
- Design score: 4 / 5
Poco F9 Ultra review: Display
- Large, bright 6.9-inch panel
- Up to 185Hz refresh rate in some games
- Punch-hole selfie camera
The Poco F9 Ultra’s display is excellent, with great brightness and clarity. It's a 6.9-inch 1200 x 2608 AMOLED panel that Poco claims has a peak brightness of 10,000 nits, much higher than rivals. However, it tames that claim by saying this 10,000-nit figure only applies to 1% of the display area, so a 4,500-nit “multi-scenario peak brightness” is the real figure here.
This is a good example of a brand obfuscating the real specs when it doesn’t need to. The F9 Ultra has a great screen, so Poco should lean into the actual numbers rather than fudging a fake one for marketing purposes. The display is very easy to read in bright sunlight, which is all you need to know.
Poco offers excellent granular control over display and color settings, a nod to the phone's gaming focus under the hood. You'll find ‘Original color PRO’ or ‘Vivid’ options in the settings app, which offer full custom control so you can find the right look for you. A dedicated hardware chip can even enhance video quality if you switch the ‘dual-core visuals’ toggle on. All this really does is smooth everything out, so I left it off.
The display can refresh at up to 185Hz, which is the highest I have ever tested on a phone. Most modern OLED displays achieve 120Hz with a variable rate, and some gaming phones have pushed to 144Hz or 165Hz. At the time of writing, the F9 Ultra's 185Hz rate is only available in CrossFire: Legends and Blood Strike, but you'll still get 165Hz in titles like Call of Duty: Mobile and Bang Bang.
So again, what Poco should really say here is that the F9 Ultra has an excellent 120Hz display in most scenarios. That information is hard to come by in the review documents I was provided with, and most users, most of the time, will never see 185Hz unless they play the two aforementioned games daily.
I personally prefer the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s display, which I think handles white balance better and isn’t so blinding to look at, but it’s a close call, and the F9 Ultra certainly has one of the best displays for the price. It’s a great choice for a large screen and undercuts, say, the Galaxy S26 Plus by a significant margin, though the F9 Ultra's display has a slightly lower resolution.
With every conceivable display spec under the sun included here, such as HDR10+, Dolby Vision, and TÜV Rheinland certification for flicker-free viewing and blue light filtration, it’s hard to criticize the screen on this phone.
- Display score: 5 / 5
Poco F9 Ultra review: Cameras
- Strong 200MP main lens
- Very capable 5x telephoto
- Ultra-wide is not the best
Poco has equipped the F9 Ultra with a pleasingly capable trio of cameras, which is led by a 200MP main lens, an upgrade on the 50MP shooter on the F8 Ultra. Shots are binned down to 12.5MP by default, though 50MP and 200MP settings can be toggled on.
In the default mode, shots look excellent, offering most of the color and mood I personally like from Xiaomi phones such as the Xiaomi 17 Ultra and 17T Pro, though Poco does not have the same Leica partnership or photo filters here.
Apart from a few times where colors looked wildly oversaturated, I really liked the output from the F9 Ultra. It has an artistic, filmic quality that many phones abandon in 2026 in favor of sharpened, contrast-heavy looks. The main camera is better than that of the regular Galaxy S26, which retails for $899 / £879, $100 / £20 less than the Poco.
It’s great to see a 5x optical zoom lens here too, mirroring what you’ll find on the Xiaomi 17T Pro and beating the S26’s 3x optical lens handily. Images are crisp thanks to optical image stabilization (OIS), and shooting in portrait mode at 5x makes for some great street photography. The F9 Ultra is also a phone that’ll come in handy when you’re sitting up in row Z at your next Harry Styles concert thanks to digital zoom up to 100x, though things look patchy after 30x.
The 50MP ultra-wide lens is the weakest of the three cameras, but that’s usually the case on triple-lens phones. In broad daylight, images are very usable, but without OIS, the smaller sensor size shows its limitations in low light, with noise and grain.
The 32MP selfie shooter is solid for solo and group snaps, and works as you’d expect for video calls.
Speaking of video, the main lens can record at up to 4K at 60fps, or even 8K at 30fps. 4K 60fps is great to see, though the Snapdragon chipset here is probably capable of 4K 120fps, like you’ll find on the aforementioned Xiaomi 17 Ultra and the cheaper 17T Pro. This is a case of Poco limiting its hardware’s capabilities in software, which is a shame, even if most users won’t notice.
That said, the camera app is fully featured and well designed, with an accomplished Pro mode offering the ability to shoot in RAW for those who want to edit images later on their computer.
- Camera score: 4 / 5

Poco F9 Ultra review: Performance
- Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 is still excellent
- Nothing slows this thing down
- Bose audio is fun but not a gamechanger
Performance is where Poco phones really shine, and the F9 Ultra is the most performant Poco phone yet. Its flagship-level specs include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, though this is the same chipset as you'll find in the F8 Ultra. Poco explained this decision to us, so you can see if you agree with the firm's reasoning, but it does appear as though the launch of the F9 series was brought forward this year, because Poco has opted to not use the next-generation flagship Snapdragon chipset, which is usually unveiled in October.
The base $799 / £899 F9 Ultra comes with 12GB RAM and 256GB storage, though there are also 512GB and 1TB storage options available, each offering 16GB RAM. Poco sent me the latter for review, which retails for £1,199 — notably less than the 12GB/256GB Galaxy S26 Ultra, which is £1,279. So, despite some price rises, Poco is still delivering value here for those after the very best specs for the money.
Performance follows, too. I could not get the F9 Ultra to stutter, even when playing Genshin Impact with the settings maxed out — the Pixel 11 Pro XL, by contrast, can’t even load the game.
The impressive thing about the F9 Ultra is its sustained performance under load. Where rival phones can stutter after half an hour or so on Call of Duty: Mobile, the Poco soldiers on (pun intended) without breaking a sweat. The phone didn't overheat once during my time testing it, presumably thanks to the built-in cooling system that Poco says reduces strain on the CPU.
Audio is great thanks to two stereo speakers and the addition of a subwoofer next to the cameras. This is tuned by Bose thanks to a partnership, and promises deeper bass and a wider soundstage. Compared to the Pixel 11 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus, the Poco F9 Ultra sounds much fuller when playing music out loud or listening to gaming audio, though I don’t think this is a reason to buy the phone. The Bose partnership improves audio slightly, but you will still want headphones connected via Bluetooth for most things.
Now that you can no longer buy the identically priced OnePlus 15 in the US or UK (RIP), the F9 Ultra would have been your best bet for Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5-level power, but the previous-gen F8 Ultra offers incredibly similar performance and is available at the time of publication for £649.
- Performance score: 5 / 5
Poco F9 Ultra review: Software
- HyperOS 3 based on Android 16 at launch
- Some AI tools require account sign in
- Four years of Android updates, six of security
The F9 Ultra gets Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3 Android skin, which at launch is based on Android 16, rather than the latest version, 17. Poco says the phone will get four platform updates, presumably to Android 20, and six years of security updates to keep buyers going until 2032.
HyperOS changes the look of Android to feel a little more like the iPhone’s iOS, but that’s no bad thing as it is perfectly functional, if a little cluttered at times. It’s a shame to see bloatware installed on a phone of this price, with AliExpress, Amazon Music, TikTok, and a few others pre-installed, but they can all be removed.
Going the way of iOS, notifications are a swipe from the left while quick settings are from the right. After I’d wrangled the software a bit during setup, I got it looking cleaner with more icons per row and fewer folders full of apps that are initially presented.
What is thankfully not shoved in your face is AI, even though there is a lot of it on board. There’s a whole section in the settings app called Xiaomi HyperAI, which directs you to Google’s built-in Gemini platform, as well as Xiaomi’s own branded AI tools.
AI Dynamic Wallpapers, AI Writing to generate text, AI Speech Recognition to transcribe audio, AI subtitles for videos — AI everything! In the Gallery app, there are some capable AI editing tools, including a beautify mode that works well. But others, such as an Ultra HD toggle or an Expand feature to generate images, require you to sign in to a Xiaomi account within the settings app.
HyperOS is visually quite different to Google’s Android flavor on the Pixel or the now-barely-seen ‘stock’ Android look, but I’ve warmed to it in recent months. It’s perfectly functional, and mercifully lets you swipe down on notifications to expand them, unlike on fellow Xiaomi stablemate Redmi’s phones.
The software is also very responsive on this hardware. Menus flow, and apps open instantly. I saw and felt no difference between the F9 Ultra and other, more expensive Android flagship phones. It feels faster than Samsung’s S26 series in many ways, though that could be down to Samsung’s slower default animations.
- Software score: 4 / 5
Poco F9 Ultra review: Battery
- Two- to three-day battery life
- 100W fast charging but no charger in UK box
- 50W wireless and 27W reverse wired charging
The F9 Ultra has a whopping 8,050mAh silicon-carbon battery. This new tech means phone makers can put higher-density batteries in phones than they could with lithium-ion, resulting in devices of the same physical thickness that last for much longer. Using the F9 Ultra as my main phone for more than a week, I consistently got two days of use out of it, sometimes stretching into a third day’s morning.
That’s seriously good longevity, made even more impressive by the phone’s flagship specs. It’s capable of 100W wired charging, but there is frustratingly no charger in the box for UK buyers. I tested the charging speed of the F9 Ultra using a Vivo 100W charging brick with the ‘Top Speed’ charging setting turned on.
The phone went from dead to 100% in 95 minutes, which is impressive for a battery of this size, and it got to 27% in 15 minutes. You’ll have to fork out for a compatible fast charger, which is a little galling when you’re laying down at least $799 / £899.
The phone also has 50W wireless charging — faster than the S26 Ultra can do via a wired connection (45W) — and can even be used as a power bank for other devices thanks to 27W wired reverse charging and 22.5W reverse wireless charging.
A few phones on the market go for longer, like the Redmi Note 17 Pro Max, but the Poco F9 Ultra gets top marks here for stonking battery life paired with top-tier specs.
Here are the phone's charging speed results broken down:
- In 15 minutes: 27%
- In 30 minutes: 46%
- 0-50%: 33 minutes
- 0-100%: 95 minutes
- Battery score: 5 / 5
Should you buy the Poco F9 Ultra?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
| Value | The Poco F9 Ultra offers top specs for a lower price than many of its competitors, but the F8 Ultra has the same chip for less. | 4/5 | 
| Design | While a refinement on the F8 Ultra, the design is sleek and is as manageable to hold as large phones get. | 4/5 | 
| Display | A superlative 185Hz display that usually tops out at 120Hz, save for some games. Great peak brightness and extensive customization options. | 5/5 | 
| Software | HyperOS 3 is a mature and easy to use software skin, though launching on the older Android 16 stings. AI stays out the way if you want it to, which is a win. | 4/5 | 
| Cameras | Very capable triple cameras led by a 200MP main sensor are a year-over-year upgrade, though they rank a tier below the very best on the market. Still excellent in this price range, though. | 4/5 | 
| Performance | Incredible performance thanks to Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and up to 16GB RAM. Sustained performance under load is notably great thanks to strong thermal management. An exemplary gaming phone. | 5/5 | 
| Battery | Some of the best battery life on a phone with flagship specs thanks to enormous silicon-carbon cell and fast charging, though no charger in the box (in the UK). | 5/5 | 
Buy it if...
You want the best battery life on a flagship phone
Two days of battery life with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone is possible with this phone; you may even get three days with careful use. This is the best you can get in the UK with these specs.
You want top gaming performance
No game can bring this thing down. If you fire up triple-A mobile games every day, the F9 Ultra should be at the top of your shopping list.
You want a great, large display
There aren’t many better displays on a smartphone. It’s best suited to mobile gamers, but the 6.9-inch size is strangely manageable thanks to good handset design.
Don't buy it if...
You want to spend as little as possible on these specs
Poco sells a very similar product for less in the F8 Ultra, which is still on sale.
You want the best cameras in this price range
While very capable, you can get better cameras on the Xiaomi 17T Pro for less.
Poco F9 Ultra review: Also consider
The Poco F9 Ultra is a strong phone in its price range, but there are a couple of similarly priced options worth considering alongside it:
Xiaomi 17T Pro
This phone has very similar specs to the Poco and costs £100 less. It lacks the Snapdragon chip, but has better-tuned cameras and longer software support.
Read our full Xiaomi 17T Pro review
Oppo Find X9 Pro
A phone with noticeably better cameras and very comparable performance is on sale at the time of writing for £899, the same price as the F9 Ultra.
Read our full Oppo Find X9 Pro review

| Price: | $799 / £899 | £799 | £1,099 (£899 on sale) | 
| Display: | 6.9-inch OLED | 6.83-inch OLED | 6.82-inch OLED | 
| Cameras: | 200MP main; 50MP ultra-wide; 50MP 5x telephoto | 50MP main; 12MP ultra-wide; 50MP 5x telephoto | 200MP main; 50MP ultra-wide; 200MP 3x telephoto; 50MP 10x telephoto | 
| Chipset: | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | MediaTek Dimensity 9500 | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 | 
| Battery: | 8,050mAh | 7,000mAh | 7,050mAh | 
How I tested the Poco F9 Ultra
- Review test period: Two weeks
- Testing included: Everyday use with messaging, web browsing, social media, photography, video calling, gaming, streaming video, music streaming
- Tools used: Geekbench 6, 3DMark
☑️ 100s of smartphones reviewed
☑️ 15 years of product testing
☑️ Over 16,000 products reviewed in total
☑️ Nearly 200,000 hours testing tech
I tested the Poco F9 Ultra over the course of two weeks, using it as my main phone with my main SIM card for a week, and as a secondary phone on other days. I used it to make calls, send WhatsApp messages, take video calls, play mobile games, stream podcasts and music, and take scores of photos.
I tested the performance of the phone’s display, chipset, cameras, and battery life for this review, comparing results with Poco’s claims as well as my decade of experience reviewing Android smartphones professionally. I’ve used many of the most recent Android flagship devices the F9 Ultra is gunning for.
I also ran benchmark tests using the Geekbench 6 and 3DMark apps to qualify my performance assessments of the phone.
Read more about how we test here.

Henry is a freelance technology journalist with more than a decade of experience in the industry. Formerly Deputy Tech Editor at the Daily Express, he has also held senior positions at Tech Advisor, and has reviewed countless smartphones over the years, obsessing over screens, battery life, and camera smarts. He reviews phones, tablets, wearables and headphones, and has contributed to TechRadar, Trusted Reviews, Stuff, PC World and Macworld. He still daydreams about a time when the Game Boy Color was the bleeding edge of handheld gaming.

articles.title: GEO brauchst du nicht – meint Google
articles.text:
Sichtbar in KI-Antworten: Was Marketer jetzt über GEO wissen müssen
Damit die eigene Website trotz vermehrter Suchen mit KI-Chatbots und der Anzeige von KI-Antworten auf der Google-Ergebnisseite sichtbar bleibt, greifen viele SEO-Expert:innen zu GEO-Maßnahmen. Im Rahmen der Generative Engine Optimization werden Inhalte so aufbereitet, dass Produkte und Marken von KI-Tools erwähnt oder Websites als relevante Quelle erkannt werden.
Google: Websites brauchen kein GEO
Aus Google-Sicht brauchen sich SEO-Expert:innen diese Mühe allerdings nicht zu machen. Es gebe nichts Spezielles, was man tun könne, um in den KI-Antworten auf Google aufzutauchen, wie Googles John Mueller via Bluesky erklärte. Dort hatte zuvor ein Nutzer gefragt, ob es Branchen gebe, bei denen GEO noch keine Rolle spiele.
Ähnlich wie Mueller jetzt hatte sich Google-Kollege Brendon Kraham schon im Juni 2026 geäußert. Gute SEO sei gleichbedeutend mit guter GEO, so Kraham. Auch bräuchten Website-Betreiber:innen ihre Inhalte nicht für Bots zu optimieren und sollten sich nicht nur generischen Content wie Top-10-Listen konzentrieren.
Optimierung für die KI-Suche
Im Mai 2026 hatte Google derweil erstmals Empfehlungen für die Optimierung von Websites für die KI-Suche veröffentlicht. Darin empfahl der Konzern einmal mehr die Erstellung von hochwertigen Inhalten, wie seo-suedwest.de schreibt. Die klassische SEO habe demnach für die KI-Suche weiter Relevanz. Nicht zuletzt, weil die KI-Features in der Suche auf Googles Core-Ranking- und Qualitätssystemen basieren. Heißt: Die KI-Antworten kommen direkt aus dem entsprechenden Suchindex.
Damit ist allerdings die Frage, ob man für mehr Sichtbarkeit im KI-Zeitalter auf GEO setzen muss, nur für Googles KI-Antworten geklärt. Hier reicht – zumindest laut der offiziellen Einschätzung des Suchkonzerns – klassische SEO aus, um sich zu positionieren.
GEO statt SEO für Googles KI-Rivalen?
Ob das aber auch für die KI-Konkurrenz von ChatGPT über Claude und Perplexity bis hin zu Copilot und Grok gilt, hat Mueller nicht beantwortet. Hier könnte GEO für Website-Betreiber und Unternehmen doch noch den Unterschied machen.

articles.title: Microsoft Rolls Out Emergency Windows 11 Patch, But AMD GPU Driver and File Explorer Crashes Remain
articles.text:
Tuesday, September 15th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Microsoft Rolls Out Emergency Windows 11 Patch, But AMD GPU Driver and File Explorer Crashes Remain
Microsoft today rolled out an out-of-band emergency Windows 11 patch with KB5129195, which is being distributed to everyone. This emergency update is automatically downloading across every PC, as it fixes crucial issues and patches privilege elevation vulnerabilities. The list of fixes in this update includes a patch for CVE-2026-62721, issues with remote desktop connection, and importantly, a partial fix for faulty USB audio. If readers recall, Microsoft's previous September update disrupted USB audio output on many PCs, affecting USB Audio Class 1.0 devices, where systems that used to work produced no sound. In the latest patch rolling out today, Microsoft noted that 8-channel and 3D audio modes are being fixed, but several other issues remain. For example, the lack of volume controls and the complete lack of audio output are still present for some USB audio devices, so this release doesn't completely fix the problem.
Next, there are a few unconfirmed issues in the previous KB5124008 September update that sites such as Windows Latest are tracking. Today's out-of-band KB5129195 doesn't fix them. These include issues with AMD Radeon GPU users, who are reportedly experiencing system freezing, crashing, driver timeouts, black screens, missing display output, and even immediate errors after reinstalling the driver stack. Separately, Windows Latest also spotted users complaining about File Explorer failing to start or crashing immediately, as well as not being able to access file history. This issue is present in some enterprise environments such as Citrix UPM, FSLogix, Horizon, or ProfileUnity ProfileDisks on both Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2.Possibly, the focus on security issues has resulted in Microsoft introducing many new bugs into the operating system, as the age of AI has brought down the wall that defended Windows before. With the help of internal AI tools to fight AI-introduced system vulnerabilities, Microsoft is rolling out security patches. However, in the process of fixing them, the OS is constantly breaking, just as we see today. Windows Latest also compiled a list with a number of CVE patches fixed, and if readers recall, it was nearly 1,000 patches applied a few days ago.

articles.title: Durante décadas creímos que los Diplodocus vivían solo en América. Acabamos de encontrar uno en Teruel
articles.text:
Durante décadas, todos los Diplodocus que conocíamos se habían descubierto en el oeste de Estados Unidos, donde se puede encontrar un gran yacimiento que nos ha dado mucha información de este dinosaurio con un característico cuello largo y una cola también en forma de látigo. Pero esto ha cambiado completamente, porque en España hemos encontrado uno de estos dinosaurios, y ya está está expuesto en un museo.
Se ha publicado. Tal y como ha recogido El País, un nuevo artículo publicado en la revista Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology ha confirmado este primer registro del género Diplodocus fuera del norte de América, abriendo la puerta a la investigación y la búsqueda de especímenes que creíamos encapsulados en un punto geográfico concreto.
Este hallazgo procede del yacimiento de La Tejería, situado en el municipio de El Castellar (Teruel). Allí, los paleontólogos han recuperado un conjunto excepcionalmente conservado de restos caudales de este tipo de dinosaurios, y concretamente 14 vértebras de la cola y varios chevrones, que son los huesos con forma de "Y" situados en la parte inferior de las vértebras.
Su presencia. Algo que sabemos ya es que este espécimen habitó la península ibérica hace aproximadamente 150 millones de años, durante el Jurásico Superior, una época en la que la geografía de nuestro planeta era muy distinta a la actual.
Los métodos. Saber que estos fósiles que se han encontrado en Teruel pertenecen a este tipo concreto de dinosaurio no es fácil. Aquí los investigadores no se han limitado a buscar un parecido superficial, sino que han identificado el material mediante complejas comparaciones anatómicas y análisis filogenéticos.
Y aquí la clave está en los detalles, puesto que los restos turolenses presentan una combinación única de rasgos anatómicos con cavidades neumáticas grandes en las vértebras, profundos surcos longitudinales en su cara inferior, chevrones bífidos con fosas mediales y cuerpos vertebrales alargados sin crestas laterales.
No es pequeño. Algo que se debe destacar aquí es que lo que se ha rescatado es principalmente parte de la cola y no el esqueleto completo del dinosaurio. Pero la realidad es que las proporciones de las vértebras permiten hacer cálculos para conocer las dimensiones que tuvo el dinosaurio cuando estaba viviendo en la península ibérica. En concreto, lo que se estima es que alcanza unos 25 metros de longitud.
Reescribimos la historia. Estamos ante una noticia bastante importante, puesto que, sabemos desde hace tiempo que la familia de los diplodócidos estaba y se han encontrado formas emparentadas en Portugal, Tanzania, Sudamérica e incluso en otros puntos de España, pero hasta este hallazgo los registros confirmados del género Diplodocus procedían de manera exclusiva de Norteamérica.
Su movimiento. Es por ello que este descubrimiento rompe el monopolio geográfico que estábamos viviendo y plantea preguntas sobre cómo se movían los dinosaurios por la geografía, y es por ello que estos restos marcan un hito importante en la migración entre continentes.
Esta presencia de un Diplodocus en Europa es compatible con episodios de dispersión intercontinental. Los paleontólogos sugieren que este intercambio faunístico estuvo posiblemente facilitado por conexiones terrestres temporales o por una reducción significativa de la barrera marina que separaba las masas terrestres en aquella época, lo que habría permitido a estos colosos expandir sus dominios mucho más allá de lo que los libros de texto nos habían enseñado.

articles.title: Android 14 provoque un énorme décalage audio sur plusieurs TV Sony BRAVIA
articles.text:
Plusieurs téléviseurs Sony BRAVIA équipés du SoC MediaTek Pentonic 1000 souffrent d'un important problème de synchronisation audio sous Android 14. RTINGS a reproduit un retard pouvant atteindre plusieurs centaines de millisecondes, notamment lors de longues sessions de jeu.
Un décalage de quelques dizaines de millisecondes entre l'image et le son peut déjà être gênant. Sur certains téléviseurs Sony BRAVIA, le problème peut aller beaucoup plus loin.
Dans une note publiée le 9 septembre, le média indique que le dysfonctionnement concerne tous les téléviseurs Sony équipés du MediaTek Pentonic 1000 sous Android 14 lorsqu’ils utilisent du LPCM via ARC.
Plus de 600 ms de retard dans certains tests
Le bug apparaît surtout après certains changements de mode vidéo, typiques d’une console ou d’un PC. RTINGS cite notamment les passages entre 4K à 60 Hz en SDR et HDR, ou encore vers du 1080p à 120 Hz. Ces changements provoquent un nouveau handshake HDMI, après lequel le son peut progressivement se désynchroniser pendant 20 minutes ou davantage.
Les mesures réalisées sont particulièrement parlantes : environ 250 ms sur le Sony A95L, 438 ms sur le BRAVIA 7 II et plus de 600 ms sur le BRAVIA 9. Ces écarts ne traduisent pas une gravité différente selon les modèles : RTINGS précise que tous les téléviseurs concernés peuvent atteindre des niveaux de retard comparables.
Le cas du BRAVIA 9 est d’autant plus intéressant que RTINGS a observé le décalage de plus de 600 ms après son passage d’Android 12 à Android 14. Certains modèles plus anciens peuvent donc avoir hérité du problème à la faveur d’une mise à jour logicielle. Le dysfonctionnement couvre donc plusieurs générations de la gamme, de l’A95L de 2023 au BRAVIA 8 II de 2025, jusqu’aux BRAVIA 7 II et 9 II de 2026.
Le problème semble venir du traitement audio des TV Sony
RTINGS évoque principalement des flux LPCM transitant par HDMI ARC/eARC, mais tout indique que la liaison avec une barre de son ou un ampli n'est pas directement responsable. Une fois le décalage apparu, celui-ci persiste en effet lorsque la barre de son est débranchée et que les haut-parleurs intégrés du téléviseur prennent le relais.
Le problème semble donc se situer dans le traitement audio interne du téléviseur. Un autre indice va dans ce sens : RTINGS n'est pas parvenu à reproduire le bug sur des téléviseurs TCL équipés du même Pentonic 1000, y compris sous Android 14. Difficile, dès lors, d'accuser directement le SoC de MediaTek ou le système de Google.
Le LPCM n'est peut-être pas non plus le seul cas concerné. RTINGS a observé des coupures avec un flux Dolby MAT provenant d'une Apple TV sur le BRAVIA 9, mais de manière suffisamment irrégulière pour ne pas pouvoir reproduire systématiquement le comportement.
À ce stade, Sony n'a pas publiquement détaillé l'origine du problème ni annoncé de correctif. Pour les possesseurs d'un BRAVIA concerné qui jouent régulièrement via HDMI, il faudra donc surtout surveiller une prochaine mise à jour logicielle.

articles.title: iPhone Duo pode não ser o único dobrável da Apple • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
iPhone Duo pode não ser o único dobrável da Apple
Decisão pelo nome "Duo" em vez do "Ultra" teria sido tomada pensando em versões futuras, diz jornalista.
O iPhone Duo chegou na semana passada, e se você acompanhou os rumores sobre o aparelho, sabe que ele tinha outros possíveis nomes. A decisão final, que veio a público nos 45 do segundo tempo, pode estar relacionada a uma vontade da Apple de expandir para uma linha completa, com outras opções de dobráveis.
De acordo com o jornalista Mark Gurman, conhecido por antecipar informações da companhia, a Apple planeja trazer mais iPhones dobráveis futuramente. Por isso “Duo”: é um nome que facilitaria a inclusão de outros complementos.
Gurman afirma que a Apple pode trazer uma versão maior, o suposto Duo Max, uma menor, apelidada de Duo Mini, e até mesmo uma versão de entrada, algo como um iPhone Duo SE. Perceba que os “sobrenomes” parecem muito mais naturais aqui do que um “iPhone Ultra Max”.
Caso a empresa decida por seguir esse caminho, poderia criar rivais para outras opções da Samsung, por exemplo. Na última janela, a empresa já trouxe um Galaxy Z Fold 8 em formato de passaporte (o mesmo adotado pela Apple nessa versão base) e um Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, seguindo o design anteriormente usado como padrão, em barra.
Possivelmente irritando os fãs da sul-coreana, que comercializa smartphones dobráveis há sete anos, Gurman também acredita que a empresa da maçã se tornará “predominante no mercado” e, ao mesmo tempo, force o resto da indústria “a aumentar os investimentos na categoria”.
Apresentado oficialmente pela Apple no dia 9 de setembro, junto com a linha do iPhone 18 Pro, o iPhone Duo marcou a estreia da fabricante no segmento. O modelo adota a proporção mais curta, chamada de “passaporte”, e traz um corpo construído em titânio.
Na parte de displays, o dispositivo conta com uma tela externa de 5,4 polegadas e abre-se em um painel interno dobrável OLED de 7,6 polegadas com acabamento antirreflexo em nano-textura, o que contribuiu muito para a redução da visibilidade do vinco.
A ficha técnica reúne o processador Apple A20 Pro, um conjunto de câmeras duplo com sensor principal de 48 MP na traseira, uma câmera frontal de 12 MP. A interface do iOS 27 foi adaptada para as novas proporções de tela.
No mercado brasileiro, o iPhone Duo tem pré-venda marcada para começar em 16 de outubro de 2026, com início das entregas e chegada às lojas a partir de 23 de outubro. Os preços oficiais divulgados pela Apple são:

articles.title: El Tesla Semi llega a Europa casi una década después de su anuncio: todos los detalles
articles.text:
Tesla confirmó que su camión eléctrico Semi desembarcará en Europa, casi 10 años después de que Elon Musk lo presentara por primera vez. La compañía reveló las especificaciones técnicas y los planes de lanzamiento para el continente durante la feria IAA Transportation 2026, celebrada en Hannover, Alemania, cuatro años después de que las primeras unidades comenzaran a circular en Estados Unidos.
El anuncio llega en un momento en el que el transporte de mercancías sigue siendo uno de los sectores más resistentes a la electrificación. Tesla se adentra ahora en un mercado europeo donde los fabricantes de camiones consolidados ya cuentan con modelos eléctricos operativos y redes de servicio desplegadas desde hace tiempo.
PUBLICIDAD
Especificaciones técnicas del Tesla Semi para el mercado europeo
La versión europea del Semi corresponde al modelo de acceso de autonomía estándar, conocido como Standard Range. Este camión está homologado para recorrer hasta 550 kilómetros con una carga completa, transportando hasta 40 toneladas de mercancía.
Su consumo energético ronda 1 kWh por kilómetro, una cifra que Tesla destaca como parte de la eficiencia del vehículo. El camión pesa alrededor de 9.100 kilogramos sin remolque y puede sumar hasta 25 kW de toma de fuerza eléctrica, conocida como ePTO, destinada a alimentar el equipamiento a bordo.
PUBLICIDAD
La recarga se realiza mediante la red Megacharger, desarrollada por la propia Tesla. Según la compañía, este sistema puede suministrar hasta 800 kW de potencia y recuperar aproximadamente el 60% de la autonomía en apenas 30 minutos.
Pese a este despliegue de datos técnicos, Tesla todavía no confirmó los precios del Semi en Europa ni una fecha exacta de comercialización. Tampoco quedó claro si las unidades destinadas al continente se enviarán desde la planta de Nevada o se fabricarán localmente, una posibilidad que el propio Musk había mencionado en el pasado en relación con la fábrica de Berlín.
PUBLICIDAD
Un lanzamiento marcado por retrasos desde 2017
El desembarco europeo representa el capítulo más reciente de un desarrollo que se extendió mucho más de lo previsto inicialmente. Tesla presentó el Semi en 2017 y fijó como objetivo comenzar la producción en 2019.
Ese calendario se fue postergando de manera sucesiva mientras la empresa priorizaba la fabricación de celdas de batería para sus vehículos de pasajeros por sobre el proyecto del camión. Las primeras entregas reales no llegaron hasta finales de 2022, cinco años después del anuncio original.
PUBLICIDAD
El siguiente hito relevante se produjo recién en abril de este año, cuando Tesla afirmó que el primer Semi había salido de una línea de producción en serie en su planta de Nevada. Sin embargo, en la llamada con accionistas de julio la compañía se limitó a prometer que la producción comenzaría en 2026, con lo cual descartó el objetivo más ambicioso de alcanzar el máximo nivel de producción durante este año.
Ahora, desde Hannover, Tesla apunta a que las primeras entregas en suelo europeo arrancarán en 2027, aunque esa fecha todavía no fue fijada como definitiva por la compañía.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué Europa puede ser un mercado más favorable para el Semi
El historial del Semi en Estados Unidos resultó bastante modesto hasta el momento. La adopción del camión fue mínima, en parte debido a los elevados costes iniciales, a la limitada infraestructura de recarga para vehículos pesados y a la escala de las rutas de transporte estadounidenses, que suelen extenderse a miles de kilómetros entre puntos de carga.
Europa podría ofrecer condiciones más favorables para este tipo de vehículo. Los países del continente son, en términos generales, más pequeños que Estados Unidos, lo que se traduce en corredores de transporte más cortos y predecibles.
PUBLICIDAD
A esto se suma que la red de recarga europea se encuentra en un estadio más avanzado que la estadounidense, un factor determinante para la operatividad de camiones eléctricos de gran tonelaje. Estas condiciones podrían permitir que el Semi de Tesla funcione bajo un escenario más realista que el que enfrentó en su mercado de origen.
PUBLICIDAD
